doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Longer phrases lately; variety versus Art Tatum
summary: He now plays longer sixteenth-note phrases than before, describing it as no barrier and a gift.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: [Scats] You know I just keep going. And it’s not about playing a lot of notes but I can do that and I show students, “Look, a good lick, Miles Davis played [scats]” — it sounds hip but it’s just as good as playing twenty notes. The other weird thing for me, and again I’m not bragging about it I just told a few people, if they even understand, something happened to me. You get older and things change, just life experience, I can’t even explain it. But maybe in the last ten years, I can’t even measure that. I can play long on piano and saxophone, long sixteenth note phrases. Whereas before I copied Sonny Stitt or whoever, and I had his licks plus a couple of mine, maybe I dovetailed them together but there was a stopping point, like a wall that came up [scats]. But now I can play two or three times longer. It’s like there’s no barrier. It’s like the wall got broken in the iron curtain or something. It’s crazy. And it’s not a bragging thing, I just — it’s like string players can play forever. It’s not a breath thing unless I ran out of breath. I can just play longer now and there’s more freedom. I said wow, that’s crazy. And I don’t do it on purpose but it’s just like, no barrier.
Do you think that’s more up in your head than it is figures?
